A 29-year-old woman is brought to the psychiatric emergency department in restraints after attempting
to break into a deli at midnight. She claims to have a groundbreaking idea for the shipping industry.
The patient is agitated but nonviolent, speaking rapidly and displaying distractibility as she discusses
numerous ideas. Her medical history includes depression and treatment-resistant hypertension.
Current medications are captopril, ibuprofen, and melatonin. A neurological exam is deferred due to
her agitation, but pulmonary and cardiovascular exams are normal, with mild bilateral abdominal bruits
noted. She is treated with haloperidol and diphenhydramine and admitted to the psychiatric inpatient
unit. After starting long-term therapy, she is discharged three days later. At a follow-up visit, her
temperature is 98.2°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 133/104 mmHg, pulse is 73/min, respirations are
16/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Chlorthalidone is prescribed, and she is instructed
to return in three days. At the next visit, her blood pressure is 135/90 mmHg. She complains of
increased urinary frequency, has a fine tremor, and her pulse is 47/min, though she remains afebrile.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Reduce the

dose of haloperidol (B) Add a beta-blocker (C) Maintain current medication regimen (D) Change
diuretics (E) Increase chlorthalidone dose (F) Refer to a cardiologist for bradycardia evaluation (G)
Monitor for diuretic-induced electrolyte abnormalities (H) Increase the dose of chlorthalidone (I) Start a
calcium channel blocker (J) Discontinue lithium therapy
 A. Increase the dose of chlorthalidone
B. Reduce the dose of haloperidol
C. Discontinue lithium therapy
D. Refer to a cardiologist for bradycardia evaluation
E. Start a calcium channel blocker
F. Increase chlorthalidone dose
G. Maintain current medication regimen
H. Add a beta-blocker
I. Monitor for diuretic-induced electrolyte abnormalities
J. Change diuretics
